en: The *Sekoddeśa*: Om, homage to Kālacakra!
Sucandra said:
The initiation is sevenfold according to the Teacher, and likewise threefold as supreme;
for the sake of attaining mundane and supramundane accomplishments, please explain it to me in brief. (Sekoddeśa 1)
The Blessed One said:

Listen, Sucandra, I shall explain to you in brief the supreme threefold [system] of seven kinds for the purpose of consecration—the movement of the channels and the vital breath (*prāṇāyāma*). (Sekoddeśa 2)
In the Tantra, the summary (uddeśa) is threefold, and the detailed exposition (nirdeśa) is likewise threefold:
the individual summary (pratyuddeśa), the great summary (mahoddeśa), and another, the individual detailed exposition (pratinirdeśaka). (Sekoddeśa 3)
The brief statement itself is the detailed explanation; this is called the recitation of the Tantra.
Furthermore, the sub-statement is the detailed explanation, which is the commentary (*pañjikā*) that analyzes the words. (Sekoddeśa 4)
The *Mahoddeśa* and the *Nirdeśa* constitute the commentary (*ṭīkā*) that indicates all meanings;
it should indeed be composed by those who have attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and not merely by scholars. (Sekoddeśa 5)
Thus, it is purified by the six parameters, by the four kinds of vajra-yogas, by the four awakenings, and by the six families of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. (Sekoddeśa 6)
The *Ādibuddha*, known by the name *Kālacakra*, is pure through five chapters concerning the world-system and other subjects, and is established by means of the two truths. (Sekoddeśa 7)
First is the sevenfold initiation which introduces the beginners;
it is threefold according to worldly convention, while the fourth is from the perspective of ultimate truth. (Sekoddeśa 8)
The teaching of phenomena by me, the Vajra-holder, is by means of the two truths:
the truth of worldly convention and the truth of the ultimate. (Sekoddeśa 9)
O King, the sevenfold consecration consists of the water, the crown, the ribbon, the vajra-bell, the great vow, together with the name and the authorization. (Sekoddeśa 10)
The purification of body, speech, and mind constitutes two empowerments each;
the permission is the purification of gnosis, while the other arises from the purification of the elements and so forth. (Sekoddeśa 11)
The water [consecration] is the purification of the elements; the crown is the purification of the aggregates;
the ribbon is the purification of the perfections; the vajra-bell is the great syllable. (Sekoddeśa 12)
The speech of the Buddha is uninterrupted; it is the purification of the sun and moon into one.
The complete purification of the objects and the sense faculties is the infallible Vajra-vow. (Sekoddeśa 13)

The purification of loving-kindness and so forth is the "Name" [initiation], and the authorization is the "Buddha" [initiation]. These seven initiations are to be bestowed after having drawn the mandala. (Sekoddeśa 14)
The vase [initiation], the secret initiation, and that which is designated as the wisdom-knowledge initiation;
furthermore, there is the great wisdom, and that which is designated as its knowledge. (Sekoddeśa 15)
The perishable, then the perishable; from that, vibration, and from that, the other, non-vibration.
Through the purification of body, speech, and mind, there is the sequence of the three empowerments. (Sekoddeśa 16)
The fourth is the complete purification of gnosis, which purifies body, speech, and mind;
it is the child, the youth, and likewise the elder, while the fourth is the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati). (Sekoddeśa 17)
Through the contact of the limbs with the breasts of Prajñā, there is the bliss of the emission of bodhicitta;
for that bliss which is attained is the consecration by the breasts of the "child" (bāla). (Sekoddeśa 18)

The bliss born after a long time from the striking of the secret [place], which is the emission of the *bodhicitta*, is the mature secret initiation, because the bliss is obtained from the secret. (Sekoddeśa 19)
From the long-term striking of the secret [place], the bliss that arises vibrates at the tip of the vajra;
he is consecrated by the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna), for that elder has attained vibration. (Sekoddeśa 20)

The bliss that arises from the passion for Mahāmudrā and so forth is "unwavering" (*niḥspanda*); he who has attained this unwavering state is consecrated with Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). (Sekoddeśa 21)
He is to be known as Prajāpati, the progenitor of all saviors;
he is Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, the non-dual, immutable Bodhisattva. (Sekoddeśa 22)
This Samayasattva is the fourfold Vajrayoga;
here it is known as Kālacakra, the bestower of liberation upon yogins. (Sekoddeśa 23)
One should perform the practice of this very [reality] through inconceivable appearances—those signs such as smoke and so forth, which are reflections of wisdom equal to space. (Sekoddeśa 24)
By means of the objects of cognition that have transcended existence and non-existence, and by one's own mind which is entirely devoid of accumulations of atoms and particles; *Sekoddeśa* 25.
Smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, and sun;
darkness, the digit, the great bindu, the universal image, and the radiant light. (Sekoddeśa 26)
That reflection which is seen like a dream in the void—by eyes that are both closed and open—and is not mentally constructed, that reflection one should always meditate upon. (Sekoddeśa 27)
In the case of non-existence, the meditation on the image is not true meditation for yogins;
for the mind perceives the image as a vision free from conceptual construction, such that it is neither existence nor non-existence. (Sekoddeśa 28)
Just as a young maiden might see a reflection of an army in a mirror,
though it is not a real thing, so too does one who is disciplined in reality perceive past and future phenomena within the sky of the mind.
Its nature is not a [conventional] existence, because it is seen as an object empty of substantial reality;
since there is no substance, the object exists like an illusion, a dream, or a magical display. (Sekoddeśa 30)
For when no substratum exists, this arising of phenomena is observed, fulfilling the infinite hopes of sentient beings like a wish-fulfilling gem. (Sekoddeśa 31)
What is unseen in the *pratisenā* [divination], such as thieves and so forth, a young girl perceives;
that the practitioners, having gone there, perceive with their own limited eyes. (Sekoddeśa 32)
If one perceives that which has the nature of existence, why does one not perceive one's own face?
If one perceives that which has the nature of non-existence, how is it that one does not perceive a rabbit’s horn? (Sekoddeśa 33)
One does not see with another's eyes, nor does one see with one's own eyes;
that which is being seen is unborn, just like the birth of a maiden.
Once the image has been seen, one should then perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) continuously by obstructing body, speech, and mind within the three channels above and below. (Sekoddeśa 35)
In those that flow as the paths of the moon, sun, Rāhu, feces, urine, and semen;
and in those born from the elements of water, fire, space, earth, wind, and consciousness—Sekoddeśa 36.
The channels of body, speech, and mind—moon, sun, and darkness—which carry feces, urine, and semen, are respectively located in the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds. (Sekoddeśa 37)
The moon is the body of skillful means, and the sun is the speech of wisdom; the feces-channel is the body of wisdom, while the urine-carrying channel is the speech of the Vīra. (Sekoddeśa 38)
Above and below, there are two mental channels: the *taminī*, which carries the mind, and the *śukravāhinī*, which carries the semen.
The *taminī* is the mind of the means (*upāya*), while the *śukravāhinī* is that of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This sixfold family, above and below, exists in all embodied beings through the union of body, speech, and mind, established by way of the factors of wisdom and means. (Sekoddeśa 40)

Inauspiciousness arises from excessive winds in the upper and lower channels of body and speech; it is the cause of birth, death, and the state of existence within the channels that carry *taminī* and semen. (Sekoddeśa 41)
At the time of birth, at death, and during sexual union, the semen-carrying channel flows; and during the solar transits at the equinoxes, the tamini channel flows upwards. (Sekoddeśa 42)
And at the junction of the rising of the ascendant, the equinox flows through the center;
it consists of fifty-six breaths and exhalations plus one quarter, O Lord of Men. (Sekoddeśa 43)
[He traverses] twenty-one thousand six hundred and seventy-five [breaths] in a day and night. (Sekoddeśa 44)
The left and right channels carry those [days] by means of the deficient mouth;
indeed, within a hundred-year lifespan, the middle channel carries them for three years and six fortnights.
Vāmā is above the left [hand], holding the moon and sun;
Lalana and Iḍā are the others, having the natures of water and fire respectively, and are considered to hold a lotus and a jewel.
Below are the two channels carrying feces and urine, whose natures are earth and wind;
the central channel and the left [channel] are considered to be the holders of the discus and the sword, respectively. (Sekoddeśa 47)
The middle channel, which flows upward, downward, and to the left, carries Rāhu and semen;
these two have the nature of emptiness and primordial wisdom, and are considered to be the holders of the vajra and the holder of the vajra. (Sekoddeśa 48)
The *viṇnāḍī* [channel] is by way of the path of the moon; the urine-carrying channel is by way of the sun;
in birth and death, at the equinox, and during passion, the semen-carrying channel is by way of Rāhu. (Sekoddeśa 49)
That which is above the navel is the *avadhūtī*, the *suṣumnā*, which carries darkness; that which is below is the *khagamukhā*, the *śaṅkhinī*, which carries semen. (Sekoddeśa 50)
In the navel-lotus, the heart, the throat, the forehead, and the uṣṇīṣa-lotus, she flows through dissolution as earth, water, fire, wind, and space. (Sekoddeśa 51)
Emerging and entering through emanation, she enters the earth;
the coming and going of the avadhūtī proceeds from one pericarp to the middle of another pericarp. (Sekoddeśa 52)
Flowing through the body, speech, and mind at the navel, the secret place, and the jewel-lotus, she emerges and enters, having the nature of withdrawal and emanation. *Sekoddeśa* 53.
The Śaṅkhinī is the channel that carries the downward-moving wind (apāna-vāyu) for all living beings;
in women, it flows with semen during pleasure and with blood during the menstrual period. (Sekoddeśa 54)
By virtue of being the limbs of wisdom and means, [the channels] are above on the right and left;
below, they are the carriers of feces and urine, and the flows of menstrual blood and semen. (Sekoddeśa 55)
Caṇḍālī is known as the carrier of the female menses, while Khagamukhā is the carrier of semen; during the fertile period (ṛtu), she is called Dombī in women and Avadhūtikā in men. *Sekoddeśa* 56.
The five mandalas beginning with consciousness always flow in the left channel;
those beginning with earth flow in the right channel; and the sixth flows in the middle. (Sekoddeśa 57)
On the petals of the navel lotus, there are sixty mandalas in their respective order: on the left and right, beginning with Aries and beginning with Taurus. *Sekoddeśa* 58.
Then, in sequence, wind [arises] from the base on the left, then on the right, then upwards, and in the middle;
one by one, the mandalas of earth and the other elements emerge from the staff-like [central channel] through the two nostril apertures. (Sekoddeśa 59)
A single nāḍī sequentially carries three hundred and sixty breaths;
five nāḍīs carry those one thousand eight hundred breaths. (Sekoddeśa 60)

Sixty nāḍīs constitute a day and night, which correspond to the maṇḍalas within the body; they are located in the center of the petals, then in the east, right, left, and west, respectively. (Sekoddeśa 61)

Space and the others are always on the left; earth and the others are on the right from the other [side]. On the left is the emanation beginning with consciousness; on the right is the withdrawal beginning with earth. (Sekoddeśa 62)
Others [hold that] earth and wind, wisdom and means, are mutually [related];
for by means of both the thumb and the ring finger, there is the sprinkling upon the mouth. (Sekoddeśa 63)
The oblation on the right and the water on the left are wisdom and means respectively;
because the sword will be formed by both the middle and index fingers. (Sekoddeśa 64)
The mudrā has the shape of a half-moon; the fangs are the razor-edged blade at the little finger.
The void is the syllable above and below; wisdom and means are mutually interdependent.
When the ten circles of the fingers are joined together with one another, and the palms are hollowed out above the head, it is the single-pronged [vajra] with the knife. (Sekoddeśa 66)
That equinox, which effects creation and destruction, resides in the central channel;
it is the unification of the aggregates, elements, and the three vajras upon entering the central channel. (Sekoddeśa 67)
When the lunar and solar channels are obstructed, the channels of feces and urine are obstructed;
when the channel of Rāhu is obstructed, the downward-flowing channel of semen becomes obstructed. (Sekoddeśa 68)
When [the breath] is released, these channels that effect creation and destruction become released;
this is the movement of the channels through the three paths of prāṇa and apāna. (Sekoddeśa 69)
If the wind flows excessively in either the left or the right [nostril] for one night, five nights, or three nights, death follows thereafter. (Sekoddeśa 70)
Five, ten, twenty, twenty-five, and thirty-three; this is the ascent of the days in sequence, which constitutes the fatal sign (*ariṣṭa*) when the sun is in the southern course. (Sekoddeśa 71)

The lifespan of embodied beings passes away in three, two, or one months, and in sixty, thirty, twelve, ten, five, three, two, or one days; [and] in fifteen, ten, five, three, two, or one fortnights. (Sekoddeśa 72)
From the root, the ascent of the moon occurs on the left by an increment of one;
it proceeds for days and months, for days and months, [lasting] three days and two months.
On an auspicious day and in a favorable month, there is increase for both; however, from that point, there is decline.
The ascent toward death occurs gradually until the completion of one hundred years.
Then, by means of the mandalas of his days—both even and odd—the ascent occurs on the right and the left, through the destruction of both wings. (Sekoddeśa 75)
Otherwise, death would not occur because the two sides would remain unestablished;
[death occurs] due to the movement through the left and right [channels] and the flow of the five maṇḍalas. (Sekoddeśa 76)
Having recognized the signs of death, one should cause the vital breath to enter the *bindu*;
relying upon the state of the *avadhūtī*, one should meditate on the supreme syllable.
One should always effect the vajra-arising by obstructing the movement of the moon and the sun;
otherwise, the vital wind does not enter the channel of Avadhūtī. (Sekoddeśa 78)

The downward-moving breath (apāna) flows below into the Śaṅkhinī; from its non-entry there occurs death. Indeed, this is the deception of the omens of death (ariṣṭa) for yogins, which occurs through the blisses. (Sekoddeśa 79)
The arrival of the semen at the joy [of bliss] occurs from the uṣṇīṣa to the lotus of the ūrṇā;
supreme joy occurs at the throat and the heart, and from there, the joy of cessation arises. (Sekoddeśa 80)
When the various delights that have arisen in the navel reach the secret lotus, and from the secret place up to the vajra-jewel, that is the unchanging innate bliss. (Sekoddeśa 81)
Non-abiding nirvāṇa is great passion, the immutable Lord;
that bliss which falls away from passion is a nirvāṇa that abides. (Sekoddeśa 82)
The rising of the moon of semen occurs at the crown; it is full in the secret lotus.
That which is the sixteenth digit resides at the top of the vajra in the jewel-lotus.
Beyond that, at the arrival of the first day of the dark fortnight, there is the time of death;
the sun quickly reaches the state of dissolution due to detachment on the new moon day.
His sixteenth digit has gone to the uṣṇīṣa lotus;
here he is called the "lost moon," detached from the bliss of passion. (Sekoddeśa 85)
At death, for all embodied beings, the lunar nectar descends below,
while the solar dust and the consciousness of Rāhu ascend above at the moment of the characteristic of existence.
Therefore, O King, the movement of the lunar nectar should be directed upwards, and that of the solar dust downwards, into the syllable of bliss which is the gnosis of Rāhu. (Sekoddeśa 87)
In the *ūrṇā*-lotus of all Buddhas, there is the full moon of nectar;
in the secret place, the sun-dust; and in the *uṣṇīṣa* and the jewel, the two [of those]. (Sekoddeśa 88)
Thus, the Vajra-word of the Teacher is the opposite for all embodied beings;
because of non-abiding nirvāṇa, the elements go toward what is the opposite. (Sekoddeśa 89)
The mind is in the jewel, speech in the secret place, and body at the navel; from the great bliss, these—Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies—radiate forth from the pure body. (Sekoddeśa 90)
O King of Kings, the lower means is below, while wisdom is above;
the Vajra of Body of this [wisdom] is located in the lotuses of the forehead, throat, heart, and navel. *Sekoddeśa* 91.
These vajras of speech, mind, and gnosis emanate from the nirmāṇakāya and the others; their emanation arises from the bliss of the aggregates and elements being free from obscuration. (Sekoddeśa 92)

Through union with the action-seal (karmamudrā), by means of relying on the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā), and through the singular yoga of the great seal (mahāmudrā), that immutable [bliss] increases. (Sekoddeśa 93)

For that which has increased, there is no further increase; for that which has diminished, there is no further diminution. For that which has set, there is no setting; for that which has risen, there is no rising. (Sekoddeśa 94)
Light does not arise from light, nor is darkness concealed by darkness;
there is no birth for that which is already born, and no death for that which is already dead. (Sekoddeśa 95)
For one who is liberated there is no liberation, and for one who does not abide there is no non-abiding;
for there is no non-existence of non-existence, nor indeed existence of existence.
Even for the perishable, there would be no perishing; nor for the imperishable, would there be imperishability.
For phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, there is the arising and likewise the destruction of illusion. (Sekoddeśa 97)
Beings do not undergo destruction, nor are they born by way of intrinsic nature;
this universe is devoid of intrinsic nature, characterized solely by existence and non-existence. (Sekoddeśa 98)
The mind embraced by one’s own wisdom has entered the vajra-jewel within the lotus;
there, the movement residing in the moon is the meditation on the motionless syllable. *Sekoddeśa* 99.
The cultivation of body, speech, and mind occurs within the channels of body, speech, and mind;
the integration of the three vajras is the cultivation of gnosis within the Śaṅkhinī. (Sekoddeśa 100)
And for the drops melted by the passion of wisdom, which have entered the state of fullness from the head in succession, there is binding in the ultimate sense. (Sekoddeśa 101)

Just as the moon, as described, reaches fullness through its digits in due order, so too is there the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); the "full moon" is the cutting away [of obscurations], not a filling [of them]. (Sekoddeśa 102)
Thus, the knowledge arisen in sequence reaches fullness through the stages (*bhūmi*);
the removal of afflictions and so forth, and the cutting off of ignorance regarding the full [stages], is not "filling. (Sekoddeśa 103)
Just as the moon is not stable when full by the mark of the middle moon, so too the mind is not stable in immutable bliss by the mark of the latent tendencies of saṃsāra. (Sekoddeśa 104)
Arising and dissolution, the white and black fortnights are established;
but that which is full between those two is full and not established. (Sekoddeśa 105)
When the mind [is established] in the vajra-jewel, it becomes motionless at the full [moment]; that is the awakening in a single moment which fulfills all moments. (Sekoddeśa 106)
There is no abiding for it in the bright fortnight, nor any going anywhere in the dark;
situated in the middle of both fortnights, it has gone to non-duality in the full moon. (Sekoddeśa 107)
Its arising from the uṣṇīṣa reaches fullness at the vajramaṇi;
through passionlessness there is a loss of digits, and through the emission from the vajra there is fullness. (Sekoddeśa 108)
For there is indeed an arising again at the uṣṇīṣa, and it becomes full once more at the vajramaṇi;
through the fading away of passion, there is a loss of digits, but no loss of gnosis for embodied beings. (Sekoddeśa 109)
Its nature of great bliss is expressed by the word "full" (pūrṇā);
all other various states are caused by creation and withdrawal. (Sekoddeśa 110)
From existence one goes to nirvāṇa, and from that one returns to rebirth; just as the moon [moves] by its two phases, or as the sun [moves] by its two solstices. (Sekoddeśa 111)
When [the breath] is full, there is the complete perfection of this immovable state through twenty-eight hundred and two breaths consumed in moments of the imperishable. (Sekoddeśa 112)
Having transcended the two sides, it is perfected through the stages;
it is the meaning of the truths in twelve aspects, the imperishable in sixteen aspects. (Sekoddeśa 113)
The mind, which is supreme non-duality, is filled with twelve aspects by means of the stages; it is the sixteen-aspected imperishable, filled with its digits. (Sekoddeśa 114)
The mind has reached the state of fullness, being completely filled; it is the single reality, non-dual, the ultimate truth, and indestructible. (Sekoddeśa 115)
The great passion beginning with dispassion, the Vajra-Anaṅga, the great imperishable, which is completely full and untainted by the latent impressions of the two sides. (Sekoddeśa 116)

Just as river water that has entered the ocean becomes identical to its water, so too this collection of phenomena, having entered the Imperishable, becomes identical to that Imperishable. (Sekoddeśa 117)

Just as this collection of elements, when consumed, attains the state of taste, and seeds attain the nature of seeds at the time of fruition, free from [the perception of] a person; so it is with the mind. *Sekoddeśa* 118.
In this way, even the aggregate of phenomena, when consumed by the supreme syllable, attains the state of the supreme syllable while assuming the nature of all forms. (Sekoddeśa 119)

When the poison has reached its full state, the bitten person feels no pain at the site of the bite, nor anywhere else; likewise, he perceives no sense objects through the doors of the senses. (Sekoddeśa 120)
Thus, when the full digit has entered the mind, the yogi perceives true bliss neither in the jewel nor elsewhere, nor does he perceive sense objects through the doors of the senses. (Sekoddeśa 121)
Just as a great elixir situated even in a single part of iron will permeate the iron from all sides when it has been heated by a fierce fire. (Sekoddeśa 122)
Even when situated in a single location, the mind—which is blissful and imperishable—is pierced on all sides by the fire of desire when it is scorched by passion. (Sekoddeśa 123)
Just as there is no stain whatsoever in pierced metals, so too there is no latent predisposition whatsoever in pierced minds. (Sekoddeśa 124)
For iron that has attained the state of gold becomes stainless through fire;
likewise, the mind becomes increasingly stainless through the fire of passion. (Sekoddeśa 125)

Just as a stone attains a state of blazing radiance through contact with a great jewel, so indeed does the mind attain a state of bliss through contact with the bliss of the immutable. *Sekoddeśa* 126.
What is the use of saying much more here? According to the conventional truth of the world, the true nature of the essence of mercury regarding the piercing of iron is inconceivable.

The true nature of gnosis is indeed to be contemplated; how much more so, then, its penetration into the mind that is stained by adventitious impurities from the perspective of ultimate reality? (Sekoddeśa 128)
The adventitious stain is not in the mind, nor has it existed in the mind for a long time;
it is not born apart from the mind, nor does it abide within the mind as something imperishable. (Sekoddeśa 129)
If the mind were merely adventitious, then it would be stainless from the beginning;
since it has existed for a long time, how could that [stain] arise from the mind itself? (Sekoddeśa 130)
If it were born without the mind, then it would be like a flower in the sky;
if it were always present within the mind, then it would never perish in any way. (Sekoddeśa 131)
Just as the blackness of copper is destroyed by contact with a chemical elixir, yet its essential nature—which exists in a state of purity—is not destroyed; [so it is with the mind]. (Sekoddeśa 132)
In the same way, the impurity of the mind perishes through union with emptiness; its nature as gnosis, which abides in purity, does not perish. *Sekoddeśa* 133.
Just as iron pierced by mercury does not return to the state of iron, so too the mind pierced by bliss does not return to the state of suffering. (Sekoddeśa 134)
There is no sin greater than dispassion, and no merit greater than bliss;
therefore, O King, one should always cause the mind to enter into immutable bliss. (Sekoddeśa 135)
Bliss cannot be described by a maiden without sexual union;
having attained sexual union in youth, she knows great bliss for herself. (Sekoddeśa 136)
Thus, it cannot be described as happiness by those devoid of meditative concentration; having attained the immutable within concentration, yogins experience it by themselves. (Sekoddeśa 137)
Even by the omniscient ones, doubt is entertained regarding the gnosis of the bliss born of the syllable;
likewise, detachment should never be cultivated toward the mind, for it is devoid of bliss. *Sekoddeśa* 138.
From death arises dispassion; from dispassion arises suffering;
from suffering comes the destruction of the elements for men; and from that destruction, death is said to occur. (Sekoddeśa 139)
For them, death leads again to rebirth; existence is death, and death is again emergence.
Thus, for sentient beings, existence arises from detachment, and not otherwise.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the passion of emission, by which the yogi attains immutable bliss and liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra. (Sekoddeśa 141)
Even a lustful person, through detachment, does not seek out the treatises on erotics; how much less would a yogi, when this Tantra has been taught by me, seek out suffering? (Sekoddeśa 142)
One should accomplish the supreme syllable by means of the nature of the immutable seminal essence;
when the support undergoes emission, there is detachment of that which is supported.

As long as the relationship between the support and the supported has not reached the state of the unchanging, the mind that has attained the state of the unchanging is no longer characterized by support and supported. (Sekoddeśa 144)
O King, for the body arisen from the syllable situated within the ūrṇā-cakra, the union of *āli* and *kāli* is not intended as the syllable *hūṃ*. *Sekoddeśa* 145.
The image arises from emptiness as the cause; the result is the bliss born of the immutable.
The cause is sealed by the result; the result is sealed by the cause. (Sekoddeśa 146)
Emptiness holding the image is the cause; compassion holding the syllable is the fruit. That which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion is the bodhicitta, the immutable. *Sekoddeśa* 147.
The image devoid of nirvāṇa is the imperishable that transcends saṃsāra; liberated from both eternalism and nihilism, its union is therefore non-dual and supreme. (Sekoddeśa 148)
There is no non-existence of the reflection, because its characteristic is to arise from non-existence;
there is no existence even of the syllable, because its characteristic is to be produced from existence. (Sekoddeśa 149)
The union of existence and non-existence is the vajra-yoga, the other non-dual [reality], free from form and formlessness, like a reflection in a mirror. (Sekoddeśa 150)
The Bimba does not enter into existence, nor does it enter into the imperishable Nirvāṇa;
mutually embraced, peaceful, it is the supreme neuter state. (Sekoddeśa 151)
Because the cause of wisdom is unborn, the fruit arises from the cause of wisdom;
because the cause of wisdom is unborn, that which is born of wisdom is not born of a cause. (Sekoddeśa 152)
Therefore, the supreme gnosis of wisdom is not born from a cause;
there is no mutual sealing by means of cause and fruit. (Sekoddeśa 153)
Whatever exists as cause and fruit, all that is dependently originated; it is a reflection sealed by mutual dependence, neither arisen nor ceased. (Sekoddeśa 154)
Wisdom is utterly extinguished, and the supreme imperishable has arisen;
it is the liberation from cause and fruit, not a mutual sealing of one another. (Sekoddeśa 155)
That which is the vision here of the knowable—neither born nor ceased—is one's own mind and not something else, due to the absence of a division into external objects of knowledge. (Sekoddeśa 156)
Therefore, it is never possible for the self to seal itself;
how can a great sword cut itself with its own blade? (Sekoddeśa 157)
Just as pleasure might arise in a dream through union with the daughter of a barren woman, so it is for the self when the image arising from space is enjoyed. (Sekoddeśa 158)
This innate [nature] is neither wisdom nor means; it is together with wisdom, completely full of bliss, and free from all obscurations. (Sekoddeśa 159)
Like space, it is unobstructed, devoid of objects and sense faculties;
it abides in all beings everywhere, indivisible and free from fragmentation. (Sekoddeśa 160)
He is the Self-Existent One, Vajrasattva, the great purpose, the supreme syllable;
he is the Great Passion, the Great Being, who brings delight to all sentient beings. (Sekoddeśa 161)
The Bodhisattva is great hatred, the destroyer of afflictions, the great enemy;
he is the Samayasattva, great delusion, who subdues the delusion of the dull-witted. (Sekoddeśa 162)
The Vajrayoga is the great wrathful one, the great enemy of the enraged Māras; Kālacakra is the great greed, the destroyer of the craving for the perishable. (Sekoddeśa 163)
The Blessed One has stated here that "vajra" means "indestructible," which possesses great significance;
it is the oneness of the three realms of existence, and is thus called the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*). (Sekoddeśa 164)
Filled with the supreme immutable bliss, perfected by the stages, he is the Great Passion, the Great Being, who brings joy to all sentient beings. (Sekoddeśa 165)
A being established in enlightenment is therefore an immovable Bodhisattva;
he is the great hatred and the great enemy of the hosts of hatred such as the afflictions. (Sekoddeśa 166)
The *samaya* is the lunar nectar, the semen; its consumption is non-emission.
By this practice, the *samayasattva* destroys the delusion of the dull-witted. (Sekoddeśa 167)
The oneness of all vajras with the syllables of the body of wisdom is the great wrathful one, the great enemy of the Māras who possess wrathful forms. (Sekoddeśa 168)
Through the means of great immutable bliss, one should never abandon the welfare of sentient beings;
possessing great passion for the sake of liberating beings, he is the destroyer of the craving for the transitory. (Sekoddeśa 169)
For these six aspects thus described—the sensations of the knowledge of the syllables, consciousness, form, formations, and perception—are your families of aggregates (*skandha*). (Sekoddeśa 170)
Fire, space, earth, wind, and water correspond respectively to the mind, the eye, the ear, the body, the nose, and the tongue. (Sekoddeśa 171)
Sound, taste, the dharma-element, smell, touch, and form—these are purified by the six families as the King of Wrath, the six-faced and fearsome one. (Sekoddeśa 172)
The body, the secret organ, and the mind are always the threefold mandala;
from the three vajras of wisdom and means, the state of Vajrasattva arises. *Sekoddeśa* 173.
This is the *sādhana* of consecration (*sekasādhana*), the *sādhana* of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*);
it is joined with the families of the channels (*nāḍīkula*) and has been spoken by the Moon according to the summary instruction (*uddeśa*). (Sekoddeśa 174)
Thus ends the glorious Sekoddeśa.
